glossary.definition: An event that could have caused harm but did not.
A rating set from the level of harm, actual or potential, defined by the organization.
An action taken to remove the cause of an incident so it does not recur.
The role accountable for decisions and records in a defined workflow.
An event that caused harm, damage, or a stoppage.
A condition someone noticed before any event occurred.
Statements that a software demonstration can prove or fail to prove, derived from the plant's own problem statement, process map, and decision table.
A step in the reporting process after which no record shows a decision was made, leaving a report unresolved.
A record showing which roles may file, read, rate, investigate, or close a report, used to evaluate whether access can be limited by role and reviewed.
A structured document recording vendor answers on setup effort, cost, and support responsibilities, used as the evaluation record for the final subsection.
A record of chosen QR code or access-point locations on the floor, including the person responsible for each and the check schedule.
The record created when a reviewer first reads a new report, showing who reviewed it, when, and what decision was made.
Fields completed by the floor reporter at the point of work, covering description, who was affected, location, time, injury or damage indicator, and optional photo.
Fields completed by the first reviewer when reading a new report, covering category and hand-off to the severity process.
Fields completed later in the process covering causes, evidence, and conclusions.
The record of the final form design stating field name, who completes it, whether it is required, and what values it accepts.

example.label: Illustrative example
example.description: An unnamed Canadian manufacturer evaluates incident and near-miss reporting software for one production area; all situations and records are hypothetical, not customer results.

reviewedChapters.title: Map how incidents and near-misses are reported today
reviewedChapters.summary: The page maps the current-state incident and near-miss reporting workflow across four subsections that match the plan exactly. All factual claims about ICC Safety capabilities are correctly framed as published descriptions requiring demonstration confirmation. The Ontario JHSC source is cited only where Ontario-specific regulatory content is discussed, with an explicit caution against assuming those rules apply nationally. Workflow elements (role, input, decision, record, exception) are present in each subsection. Illustrative examples are labeled and use an unnamed Canadian manufacturer. No FAQ section appears, which is correct because the plan assigns none. The changed paragraph correctly presents ICC Safety page content as a vendor problem description rather than measured data. No previous findings were raised. Links use the two supplied source URLs plus an allowed internal path. No scope boundary violations were detected.
decisions: Decide what counts as an incident, a near-miss, and a hazard report
Decide whether a report is accepted into the log
Decide whether corrective action is required
Decide which steps are required and which are habit
Assign a named owner and a backup to each decision
Decide which steps the software must support first

reviewedChapters.title: Evaluate incident and near-miss reporting software

The Ontario guide link is cited appropriately as one example of provincial material. Setup steps are described without overstating sequence or guarantee. No previous findings were raised and none remain unresolved. No FAQ section appears, which is correct as the plan assigns none. Workflow elements, illustrative examples, roles, records, and decisions align with the plan. No scope boundary violations, repetition issues, or readability problems were detected.

reviewedChapters.title: Design reporting intake for incident and near-miss reporting software
reviewedChapters.summary: All checks pass. The two changed paragraphs are accurate and well-scoped: the first correctly frames ICC Safety field configuration as a published description requiring demonstration confirmation and notes the anonymous-form field configurability is unconfirmed; the second gives clear procedural guidance on misuse without introducing unsupported claims. No previous findings were raised, so none remain unresolved. All factual claims about ICC Safety capabilities are hedged as published descriptions. The Ontario JHSC guide is cited with an appropriate caution about site-specific obligations. Workflow elements (role, input, decision, record, exception) are present across all four subsections. The illustrative example is labeled and uses an unnamed Canadian manufacturer. No FAQ section appears, consistent with the plan assigning none. Links use only the two supplied source URLs plus allowed internal site paths. No scope boundary violations, readability problems, or repetition were detected.
